# Performance log

Every change that affects speed or space gets an entry here: the date, the change, the workload, the numbers before and after, and the commit. Benchmarks against Syncthing come from `go run ./bench` (see `bench/README.md`).

## Setup

**Machine.** A cloud VM with 4 vCPUs (Intel Xeon @ 2.30 GHz), 16 GB of RAM, and a virtual disk (a 4 KiB `O_DSYNC` write takes about 0.16 ms), running Linux. Every process runs on this one machine over loopback; there has been no run across a real network yet.

**Corpus.** 100,000 files and 3,994 directories, 2.50 GB in all, generated by `bench` with seed 1: about 4,000 directories up to seven deep, file sizes log-normal around 4 KB, about 40% of the bytes in 28 photos and videos of 2 to 64 MB, text files that compress, and media files that don't.

**Systems.** dotfs from `dev`: one `dotfs serve` with two `dotfs sync` clients over WebSocket, with the default 1 s debounce. Syncthing v2.1.7, built from its tag with `go build` (go1.26.2), as two devices over TLS with discovery, relays, and NAT traversal off, and `fsWatcherDelayS` set to 1 to match dotfs (its default is 10).

## dotfs against Syncthing, 2026-11-19

Run at d346a52. Each cell is the final run; the range in brackets covers every run of that code (two for dotfs, two for Syncthing).

| Measure | dotfs | Syncthing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bootstrap an empty device (2.5 GB, 100k files) | **46.3 s** [44.0–46.3] | 155.2 s [155.2–171.6] |
| Change to visible, p50 | **1.01 s** | 2.28 s |
| Change to visible, p95 | **1.18 s** [1.15–1.21] | 2.29 s [2.29–2.32] |
| Change to visible, worst of 20 | 1.58 s [1.21–1.58] | 16.5 s [16.5–23.4] |
| 10,000 new 4 KiB files, A to B | 24.0 s [22.7–24.0] | **13.3 s** [11.8–13.3] |
| Reconnect after 1,000 offline changes per side | **14.2 s** [14.2–20.3] | 23.7 s [15.0–23.7] |
| Seed device A with the corpus | 212.7 s (upload to the server) | 30.8 s (scan only) |
| Index, plain and zstd | 18.7 MB and 5.9 MB, read in 0.17–0.23 s | (none) |
| Metadata on disk | server 83 MB, each client 45 MB | each device 125 MB |
| Peak RSS | server 324 MB, clients 234–311 MB | 144 MB for device B |

What the numbers say:

- **Adding a device is 3.4 times faster with dotfs.** The dotfs bootstrap reads one zstd index (5.9 MB for 100,000 paths) and fetches files many at a time.
- **A change shows up in about the debounce.** dotfs pushes a change about 10 ms after its 1 s debounce; Syncthing adds over a second more after its 1 s watcher delay, and one change in 20 took 16 to 23 s.
- **Many small files are 1.8 times slower with dotfs.** Each file is its own staged commit (commit-hash, stage, write, commit), and for each one the server fsyncs the stage file and its directory and commits a SQLite transaction. With 2,000 files the server spent about 0.7 ms of CPU per file and the client about 0.6 ms. Seeding A is the same path, at about 470 files per second. Syncthing's seed is only a local scan and does not move any data, so the two seed rows are not comparable; the bytes Syncthing moves in its bootstrap are moved by dotfs's seed.
- **Reconnecting after offline changes is about even**: both systems varied by several seconds between runs.
- **The dotfs clients hold every row in memory**, about 3 KB per file at 100,000 files. Syncthing's device A was not measured, since the benchmark looked only at the process it started, not the child Syncthing forks (fixed in `bench` afterwards).

Not measured yet: a real network, larger roots, and the kernel 9P mount.

## Entries

### 2026-11-19: sync client memory (541cc38, e8bb2ad, b840c35, and 4c6aace)

Four changes to the `dotfs sync` client: ctl replies read with a pooled 4 KiB buffer instead of a new 252 KiB one per command (`client/ctl.go`); pooled 32 KiB copy buffers and BLAKE3 hashers, with 16 KiB of spare capacity so the hasher stops allocating padded copies of each write's last chunks; the content-hash index as one path per raw 32-byte digest, with a second map only for duplicate content, instead of a set of paths per hex string; and a soft memory limit of 128 MiB (`-memlimit`, 0 for none, `$GOMEMLIMIT` wins). Full benchmark, 100,000-file corpus, on a 4-vCPU Xeon @ 2.10 GHz: two runs each of dev at c4c3455 and of these commits, and one of these commits with `GOMEMLIMIT=off` to separate the limit from the rest. Cells give the first run, then the second; the heap and allocation rows come from the first run of each, whose binaries sampled the heap every 2 s.

| Measure | Before | After | After, no limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Peak RSS, client A (seeds, then sends) | 298, 278 MB | **166, 162 MB** | 250 MB |
| Peak RSS, client B (bootstraps, then receives) | 271, 265 MB | **145, 144 MB** | 203 MB |
| Peak live heap, A and B | 210 and 219 MB | **118 and 104 MB** | |
| Bytes allocated, A over the whole run | 76.9 GB | **5.7 GB** | |
| Bytes allocated, B before its restart | 11.2 GB | **5.0 GB** | |
| Garbage collections, A and B | 1,574 and 168 | 210 and 171 | |
| Seed device A | 275.3, 271.2 s | 245.8, 241.2 s | 243.4 s |
| Bootstrap B | 56.2, 53.9 s | 53.5, 53.5 s | 52.6 s |
| Change to visible, p95 | 1.02, 1.23 s | 1.11, 1.26 s | 1.30 s |
| Change to visible, worst of 20 | 1.02, 2.18 s | 2.21, 2.53 s | 3.22 s |
| 10,000 new 4 KiB files, A to B | 28.9, 27.6 s | 26.2, 27.5 s | 25.6 s |
| Reconnect after 1,000 offline changes per side | 19.0, 18.7 s | 16.9, 18.8 s | 17.8 s |

Before, ctl reply buffers were 51 GB of A's allocations, 32 KiB copy buffers 6 GB, and the BLAKE3 hasher's padded chunk copies 3.8 GB. Peak RSS falls by about a third from the allocation fixes alone and by about 45% with the limit, which binds only briefly: the live heap peaks near it during the bootstrap's index reconcile. Seeding is about 10% faster; the other timings are within run-to-run spread. The worst change-to-visible time varies from 1.0 to 3.2 s across all five runs, old code and new, with and without the limit, so it is not from these changes. What allocates most now: `client.Upload`'s buffer per file (1.6 GB on A), `context.AfterFunc` from WebSocket read deadlines (0.6 GB), and p9's message buffers (about 0.4 GB each way).

### 2026-11-19: sync, never drop the watcher's catch-up scan (d346a52)

When the hint channel filled, the watcher tried to send its full-scan hint into the same full channel and dropped it, so changes from a burst waited for the periodic scan, a minute later. Reconnect after 1,000 offline changes per side, 100,000-file corpus: 58.7 s and 14.8 s in two runs before; 20.3 s and 14.2 s after. The dropped hint is the likely cause of the 58.7 s run, but it was not traced directly.

### 2026-11-19: sync, send runs of small files eight at a time (3435d47)

Runs of new or edited files up to 4 MiB are hashed and sent by eight workers instead of one round trip set at a time. 3,000-file corpus of 60 MB: seed 10.7 s to 6.7 s; 2,000 new 4 KiB files from A to B 7.6 s to 5.6 s. 100,000-file corpus: seed 372 s to 209 s; 10,000 new files 38.6 s to 21.8 s.

### 2026-11-19: sync, keep the commit queue's cost per change constant (9b88ca5)

`flush` rewrote the whole queue table after every queued change, so a bulk import was quadratic. 3,000 files of 350 MB: seed 65 s to 13 s. The cost grew with the square of the queue, so 100,000 files was not tried before the fix; after it, the seed took 372 s.

### 2026-11-19: integration and benchmarks (a0a2e34)

The cross-process integration tests and `bench`. No change in speed or space.

## Follow-ups

- Commit throughput for small files: batch fsyncs on the server (group commit across a scope's writer), or let a client commit several staged files in one command.
- Client memory: keep rows in SQLite and cache only what a cycle needs (rows are most of the live heap now); reuse `client.Upload`'s buffers.
- Run the benchmark across a real network, where dotfs's fewer round trips per file should matter more and its sequential large-file uploads may matter less.
